practice: Track requirements as a machine-checkable JSON feature list (not prose), each item initially marked failing, with a strongly-worded instruction that editing or removing an entry is unacceptable. Picking a cheaper planner model saves more overall than picking a cheaper worker model does ($1,339 vs $10,565 across otherwise-equal-quality mixes).

practice: To stop two independent planner agents from silently duplicating or contradicting each other's design decisions, require agents to record decisions in shared design docs, with dependent code carrying a compile-checked reference back to the deciding doc. When two docs turn out to contradict each other, a dedicated reconciler agent merges them and the references propagate the resolution downstream automatically.
notes: Same source as i3. Addresses 'contention between planners' specifically, distinct from the simpler 'split-brain' fix (i5).

practice: When many agents collide on the same files faster than any agent can absorb the others' context and merge cleanly, don't have colliding agents resolve it themselves (worker agents are bad at this and tend to overwrite or abandon their own change) — route the conflict to a neutral third-party agent whose only job is impartial, efficient resolution, the same role a merge queue plays for human teams.
notes: Same source as i3/i4. Concrete scale evidence given: old approach hit 70,000+ conflicts on one hot file before being paused; new approach saw 47 on its most-contested file over a full 4-hour run.

practice: Give worker agents a way to flag files that are becoming 'megafiles' — popular collision sites that no single agent is responsible for keeping small. Once flagged, block new commits to that file and have a separate agent decompose it into smaller modules before work resumes.
notes: Same source as i3-i5. A specific instance of a general pattern (nobody individually owns shared-resource hygiene at agent scale) worth watching for elsewhere in the corpus.

practice: Agents working in an existing codebase learn (from humans-in-the-loop precedent) not to touch core code even when it genuinely needs to change, causing stagnation. Fix by explicitly licensing intentional breakage: an agent that judges a core change worthwhile makes a focused patch outside its assigned scope with a comment explaining why, lets the compiler propagate the resulting build failures through everything that depended on the old design, and each agent that hits one of those errors reads the comment and updates its own piece to match.
notes: Same source as i3-i6. Called 'ossification' in the source. Genuinely novel coordination mechanism, not a known pattern from human team practice.

practice: No single review method catches everything, but decorrelated review lenses stack: give different reviewer agents different views of the same work (full worker transcript vs. output-only vs. nothing but the codebase) and run them on different models/training/personas. The combination outperforms any one perfect reviewer, the way redundant imperfect sensors let self-driving systems exceed any single component's reliability. Since review is much cheaper than the work it audits, this is high-return compute.
notes: Same source as i3-i7. Direct, well-reasoned justification for multi-model/multi-view review over trusting one reviewer, however capable.

practice: Give agents a shared, agent-owned folder (a 'Field Guide') whose index.md is auto-injected into every new agent at session start, that the agents themselves are responsible for curating under a hard line-budget constraint. Since model weights are frozen, the value is capturing precisely the surprising, non-obvious things a new agent would otherwise re-discover the hard way, so each successive agent's trajectory gets shorter.
notes: Same source as i3-i8. Explicitly framed by the source as an early, promising experiment, not a settled best practice yet — confidence reflects that. Directly resembles this corpus's own 'unknown unknowns' framing: capturing what a newcomer wouldn't know to ask.

practice: Give a coordinator agent the ability to break a large task into scoped pieces and delegate each to a fully isolated managed session (own VM, terminal, browser, dev environment) that verifies its own changes before reporting back, rather than one agent handling the whole task serially in a single accumulating context. The coordinator can message, monitor, or pause/terminate any managed session mid-task, and later reads the full trajectories of managed sessions to improve how it breaks down the next task.
notes: A company product-announcement post, framed favorably toward the product. The mechanism description itself is concrete and technical, so it's extracted here with that framing caveat rather than skipped.

practice: Build a three-layer, continuously-running measurement system instead of a one-time launch eval: offline benchmarks catch regressions before shipping, online A/B tests on real users show whether production behavior actually moved, and trace-clustering over failure logs explains why aggregate metrics moved (since at production scale no engineer can read every trace). No single layer is sufficient alone; treat it like the Swiss-cheese safety model, where each layer has holes but the layers together catch more than any one.

practice: Close the loop from evaluation to fixes with a self-improvement cycle run by agents, not just humans: each pass reads production logs, trace clusters, and recent failures to form a hypothesis, builds a candidate fix, opens a draft PR with its reasoning attached, measures the result against the same benchmark/A-B/trajectory data used to evaluate everything else, and recommends ship, iterate, or drop.

practice: For enterprise/team deployments, let administrators define an approved-model allowlist per workspace by policy, then have automatic per-task routing choose only from within that approved set — giving individual users hands-off model selection without giving up organizational control over which models are usable at all.

practice: Verification of agent-written code does not have to mean reviewing every line — eyeballing every line has never been the most reliable way to validate a software change in the first place; the real skill is confidently instructing the agent AND confidently verifying the result, by whatever method actually catches errors.

practice: Agents remove code-throughput as the bottleneck, but a human's cognitive capacity to stay on top of the resulting code becomes the new limiting factor — so a team still needs multiple engineers even when one person could out-produce a pre-agent team alone, to load-balance that cognitive capacity across people.

practice: The old discipline that kept software from sprawling was economic, not deliberate: a crazy feature idea got dropped because building it would take a week. Coding agents remove that cost gate, so without a DELIBERATELY imposed discipline in its place, codebases lose conceptual integrity the same way the Winchester Mystery House kept growing rooms once cost stopped constraining it.

practice: Agentic bug-finding is now fast enough that public discussion of a patch alone (no working exploit needed) draws automated exploit probing within minutes, and this has broken existing open-source security-disclosure norms built for a slower world: one maintainer went from ~20 security disclosures in 10 years to over 40 in a single month, and GitHub CVE assignment now takes 3-4 weeks instead of 2-3 days due to backlog.

practice: Wire real-time structured feedback (type-checking, linting, CLAUDE.md-compliance checks) into the tool-response itself via a post-tool-use hook, so the agent sees the equivalent of a red squiggly line at the moment of the mistake instead of discovering it later at compile or review time. practice: Put model-routing decisions in the agent harness itself, which is where the task state actually lives, instead of an API gateway in front of model providers. A gateway only ever sees a single completion request in isolation; only the harness holds the task state needed to judge a switch (session cache warmth, whether progress has stalled, how much work remains), and it must choose the model before assembling the request's tool definitions and instructions, since those differ per model family.
excerpt: Model routing belongs in the harness.
notes: Very fresh (Aug 24 2026), named author, extremely concrete with real production data over 2+ months of customer sessions: 58% aggregate cost cut vs. all-frontier baseline, 76% median session savings, turn latency 81s to 49s.

practice: Treat a mid-session model switch as a real cost decision: switching models discards the cached prompt prefix, forcing the accumulated session history to reprocess at 5-10x the cached rate. Weigh whether the current diagnostic difficulty justifies that cache-miss cost before switching to a stronger model — staying on the already-warm model is itself a routing decision, and the same switch that's cheap at turn 5 can cost over 2x an all-frontier baseline by turn 150+ if done carelessly.
notes: Includes real measured breakdown by turn-range (turns 61-150 reaching 2.12x baseline, 151-200 reaching 2.37x, when cache-blind) plus three real named session case studies with turn counts and savings percentages.

practice: When the harness spins up a subagent/worker job, choose that worker's model at the moment the job is created (as part of writing its specification), not by inheriting the parent's model or routing it later through a generic gateway. The worker starts cold (no inherited cache) but with a tight written spec instead of the full parent history, letting the parent stay on its own warm, cached model while delegating focused sub-work to a differently-tiered model.
notes: Same source as i14/i15. Real number: a measured 12-hour, 423-turn, 10-session mission saved 37.8% of total cost via this pattern vs. pricing every call at frontier rate.

practice: Deliberately pick the default reviewer/validator model from a different model family than the default implementer model, on the principle that a useful validator should fail in different places than the model it is reviewing — same-family review risks correlated blind spots.

practice: A per-rig merge-queue processor sits between completed agent work and the main branch: when an agent finishes a task, its merge request joins a queue rather than merging directly, verification gates run against each batch, and a Bors-style bisecting search isolates exactly which change in a failing batch actually broke it -- rather than trusting the completing agent's own say-so or a single human's spot-check. The isolated failure gets fixed inline or re-dispatched; nothing merges past the gate un-verified.

practice: META: an independent, large-scale observational study (20,574 coding-agent sessions across 1,639 repositories, IDE and CLI workflows) grounds why verification matters with real base-rate data rather than anecdote. Misalignment is defined as a breakdown made visible through developer pushback, sorted into seven recurring forms spanning how agents read a project, interpret intent, follow rules, bound their own actions, implement/execute code, and report progress. 90.50% of episodes cost effort and trust rather than causing irreversible damage, but 91.49% of visible resolutions still needed explicit user correction -- agents rarely self-correct a misalignment once a developer has had to notice it. Patterns differ between IDE and CLI use and persist across adjacent sessions; over time, overall misalignment rates decline, but constraint violations and inaccurate self-reporting grow in share even as the aggregate rate improves.

practice: META: an independent code-quality audit is a sharp caution against reading raw scale or throughput numbers as evidence of production-grade output. Cursor's Wilson Lin publicized 'FastRender' -- a Rust browser rendering engine built by a swarm of AI agents running for a week in January 2026, on the order of a million lines of code across roughly a thousand files by one count. Software Improvement Group's independent analysis, using an ISO 25010-based maintainability model checked against a certified reference dataset of 400+ billion lines of code, scored the resulting codebase (about 110 person-years of Rust) at 1.3 out of 5 for maintainability -- the bottom 5% of systems SIG has measured on the market. Contemporary coverage (The Register) characterized it more bluntly: the browser barely compiled and often didn't run.

practice: When doing the single deliberate read-through, scan specifically for four recurring failure shapes rather than reading generally for "does this look right": invented APIs that do not exist in the actual codebase, silent scope creep (edits the request never asked for -- a reformatted file, a renamed variable, an "improved" unrelated function), edge-case handling deleted while fixing something else, and convincing-but-wrong logic wearing a reassuring comment. On scope specifically: every hunk should trace back to the request, and anything that does not gets flagged rather than assumed intentional.
